name: Safety Technology
title: Safety Technology
answer: Safety technology covers the AI systems some vendors sell to schools for security, such as camera analytics and weapon detection. The book's research found no independent evaluation of these systems in schools, so districts should demand independent evidence and treat safety claims with the same scrutiny as savings claims. Physical safety still depends mostly on trained staff, clear procedures, relationships with students, and regular drills, which technology can support but not replace.

sections.body: This idea concerns AI products marketed for school security, including camera analytics and weapon detection. Such products can be costly and are often promoted with strong claims, yet the research gathered for this Volume found no independent evaluation of them in schools. The problem it solves is not a technical one but a purchasing and governance one: districts need a disciplined way to judge safety claims before committing money. The book directs districts to ask vendors for independent evidence and to apply the savings claim questions in this chapter to safety claims as well. It also ties these systems to the privacy and fairness questions raised by the monitoring tools discussed in Chapter 15.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a district considering a security system would first request independent evidence from the vendor rather than accept marketing claims. Because the systems collect sensitive information about students and visitors, any alert they produce should be reviewed by trained staff before anyone acts on it. The book does not give grade band guidance for this idea, so the same approach applies across a school or district. Physical safety is built mainly through trained staff, clear procedures, good relationships with students, and regular drills. Technology can support those foundations, but it cannot take their place.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with the finding that the research gathered for this Volume found no independent evaluation of these systems in schools. No study, figure, or other finding is offered beyond that absence. The text also notes that the products can be expensive and are often marketed with strong claims, which is why it recommends asking vendors for independent evidence and applying the savings claim questions in this chapter to safety claims too. On the strength of that, the idea rests on caution about unverified claims rather than on independent research showing the systems work.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set out plainly: security systems raise the same privacy and fairness questions as the monitoring tools in Chapter 15, because cameras that analyze behavior or identify people collect sensitive information about students and visitors. False alarms can cause fear, disruption, and wrongful suspicion, so any alert should be reviewed by trained staff before action is taken. Boards should be wary of spending on technology at the expense of people, since physical safety depends mostly on people and procedures. The decisions about whether to buy, how to use, and when to act stay with the district and its trained staff, not with the product.
